stories.title: The Fever’s Down, But New York’s Rent-Stabilized Market Is Still Ill
stories.excerpt: New York City’s rent-stabilized housing stock has an increasingly serious economic problem. For years, the operating expenses of these buildings have been rising much faster than their revenues. Insurance premiums, real estate taxes, water and sewer charges, fuel, labor, repairs and maintenance have all increased significantly, while the ability of owners to increase rents has been severely constrained. The Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act of 2019 eliminated or restricted many of the mechanisms owners previously used to recover investments in their buildings, and now we have a rent freeze layered on top of that. The result is not complicated. When expenses consistently grow faster than revenue, eventually the two lines cross. Robert Knakal. PHOTO: Patrick McMullan/Patrick McMullan via Getty Images New York City’s Article XI is increasingly being discussed as one possible solution. The program can provide an extraordinary property-tax benefit to qualifying buildings for as long as 40 years, replacing conventional real estate taxes with a substantially lower PILOT, or payment in lieu of taxes. For a distressed rent-stabilized building, the impact can be dramatic. A building paying 25 percent or more of its gross revenue in real estate taxes might see that burden reduced substantially. Suddenly, a property that was barely breaking even, or even losing money, can generate positive cash flow again. For an owner facing a mortgage maturity, foreclosure or the prospect of handing the keys back to the lender, Article XI can be a lifeline. But a lifeline is not a cure. Think about a patient suffering from a serious infection and running a dangerously high fever. You give the patient Tylenol. The fever comes down. The patient feels better. Everyone is relieved. But, if you haven’t treated the infection causing the fever, what happens? Eventually, the fever comes back. Article XI can bring the financial fever down, but it does not necessarily cure the und
bullets: NYC rent-stabilized buildings: operating expenses rising faster than constrained rents.
2019 Housing Stability Act eliminated owner cost-recovery mechanisms; rent freeze now in place.
Article XI PILOT program under discussion as distressed building solution.
stories.summary: New York City's rent-stabilized housing stock faces structural economics: operating costs (insurance, taxes, labor, maintenance) are outpacing revenue growth locked down by the 2019 Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act and a rent freeze. Owners have lost mechanisms to recover investments, pushing some buildings toward distress. Article XI tax abatement programs—offering 40-year PILOT relief—are emerging as a potential stabilization tool.
stories.impact: Rent-stabilized buildings becoming economically unviable creates a perverse dynamic: distressed owners may sell to consolidators or seek conversion pathways (if feasible), while developers eyeing value-add or ground-up plays in NYC must assume regulatory risk is structural, not cyclical. This tightens the universe of acquirable free-market buildings—a supply constraint on transaction volume that favors existing holders.

stories.title: Every Industry Eventually Learns a Shared Language. Data Centers Are Next.
stories.excerpt: One question has stayed with me since my last column on data center disclosure: How do standards emerge in an industry where every project is different? It is an important question because nothing about today’s data center market looks standardized. Every project is different. Every community asks different questions. Every developer tells a slightly different story. Yet history suggests that industries almost never begin with standards. They grow into them. Suhail Y Tayeb. PHOTO: Courtesy NYU The reason is straightforward. As industries mature, inconsistent information becomes expensive. Investors, lenders, insurers, regulators and customers all reach the same conclusion. Comparing projects is easier when everyone speaks the same language. The pattern repeats itself across industries. Finance eventually adopted Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) because investors needed confidence that financial statements meant the same thing from one company to the next. The standards did not make companies identical. They made companies comparable. Real estate followed a similar path. Residential appraisers do not prepare a different report for every lender. Standardized appraisal forms such as the Uniform Residential Appraisal Report, also known as Form 1004, became common because investors buying mortgages needed comparable information. The form did not standardize houses. It standardized how houses were described. Green building tells the same story. LEED began as a voluntary certification developed by the U.S. Green Building Council. Developers pursued certification because tenants, investors and lenders increasingly viewed it as a credible signal of quality and performance. Only later did many municipalities incorporate LEED into procurement requirements, incentives and public policy. Today, many data center developers proudly advertise LEED certification, Energy Star certification and corporate sustainability reports. Those certifications matter because
bullets: Data center market lacks standardization; every project and disclosure differs.
Industry history shows standards emerge as investors/lenders demand comparability.
Standardization did not homogenize real estate—it enabled transparent comparison.
stories.summary: Data center development today resembles real estate in the pre-standardization era: every project is bespoke, every community asks different questions, every developer tells a different story. The author argues standards eventually emerge when inconsistent information becomes too costly for investors, lenders, insurers, and regulators. Finance adopted GAAP and real estate adopted uniform appraisal forms for this reason.
stories.impact: Minor relevance to multifamily developers directly. However, if data center standards emerge and liquidity increases, capital flowing into standardized data center vehicles may reduce available equity and debt for multifamily—particularly institutional capital seeking comparable risk/return profiles across asset classes.

stories.title: New York City’s Next Multifamily Shortage? Buildings to Buy.
stories.excerpt: For years, nearly every conversation about New York City multifamily has centered around one shortage: housing. We don’t have enough apartments. We don’t build fast enough. Vacancy remains tight, construction is expensive, and the regulatory environment makes adding new supply increasingly difficult. But there is another shortage developing that investors and owners should be paying close attention to: a shortage of multifamily buildings to buy. I am talking about quality buildings worth buying — free-market apartment buildings with minimal regulatory risk hurdles. Lev Mavashev. PHOTO: Courtesy Alpha Realty That may sound strange after several years when buyers had the upper hand and plenty of owners struggled to get their pricing. But the market is changing. Capital is coming back faster than quality inventory is coming to market, and the numbers are starting to reflect that. According to Alpha Realty’s second-quarter 2026 multifamily market report, New York City recorded 304 multifamily transactions during the three months ended June 30, up 10.5 percent from the first quarter and 2.4 percent year-over-year. That followed 275 transactions in the first quarter, which itself was up nearly 20 percent from the prior year. In other words, despite elevated borrowing costs, transaction velocity continues to improve. Most of the multifamily transactions have been for free-market and newer construction buildings. What’s interesting is that multifamily buildings with 20-plus units accounted for 112 transactions in the second quarter, up 24.4 percent from the quarter before and 8.7 percent from a year earlier. Those assets represented $872.2 million, or roughly 57 percent of all New York City multifamily dollar volume during the quarter. That follows an already strong first quarter, when properties with at least 20 units accounted for $1.06 billion, or approximately 61 percent of citywide multifamily volume. Put those two quarters together and the message is difficult to igno
bullets: NYC multifamily transactions up 10.5% Q1-to-Q2 2026, 2.4% YoY; 304 deals in Q2.
Capital returning faster than quality free-market inventory reaching market.
Shortage of acquisitions—not housing units—now constraining buyer activity.
stories.summary: After years of buyer dominance, New York City's multifamily market is experiencing a reversal: capital is flowing back into the market faster than quality, free-market apartment buildings are coming to sale. While NYC still has a housing shortage, a separate supply constraint is emerging—a scarcity of investable buildings with minimal regulatory risk. Transaction volumes are rising (304 Q2 deals, +2.4% YoY), but inventory is not matching buyer appetite.
stories.impact: For TCR and other developers/acquirers in NYC, this signals that pricing power is shifting back to sellers of stabilized, free-market assets. Ground-up development and value-add plays become more attractive relative to stabilized acquisitions, assuming entitlements and construction costs remain feasible. Conversely, sellers holding quality free-market buildings should expect stronger bids as capital competes for limited offerings.

stories.title: Goldman Sachs to Acquire LCN Capital Partners, Expanding Sale-Leaseback Presence
stories.excerpt: Goldman Sachs said Tuesday it has agreed to acquire LCN Capital Partners, a leading investment manager specializing in the sale-leaseback, build-to-suit, and triple-net lease sectors of the real estate market, in a deal valued at up to $410 million. LCN has approximately $3 billion in assets under supervision as of June 30, 2026, primarily from institutions, insurers, and high-net-worth individuals. “LCN’s differentiated platform is highly attractive for our Asset & Wealth Management clients who want diversified sources of returns and offers corporate clients innovative capital solutions,” said David M. Solomon, chairman and CEO of Goldman Sachs. “Their focus complements our private real estate team’s broad 30-year track record and will expand our ability to serve our insurance, institutional, and wealth client segments.” LCN originates, negotiates, invests in and manages sale-leaseback, BTS and net lease investments across North America and Europe. Founded in 2011 by Edward V. LaPuma and Bryan York Colwell, New York-based LCN has raised 10 investment funds that aim to outperform credit and real estate alternatives. “Our team, our strategy, and our commitment to our partners, both capital and corporate, remain unchanged — what changes is the scale of our ambition,” said LaPuma. “By combining LCN’s origination network and investment discipline with Goldman Sachs’ unrivaled corporate relationships, global distribution, and client experience teams, we can better serve our investing and tenant partners at a scale no independent firm could match — and become an industry leading platform in triple net lease investing.” The acquisition occurs against a backdrop of significant global market opportunity for investment into sale-leasebacks, with an estimated $14 trillion of corporate-owned property on corporate balance sheets in North America and Europe alone. At the same time, investor demand for the NNN asset class is growing globally. The upfront transaction considerat
bullets: Goldman Sachs acquiring LCN Capital Partners for up to $410M.
LCN manages $3B AUM in sale-leaseback, build-to-suit, net lease.
Expands GS's institutional/insurance/wealth client access to real estate returns.
stories.summary: Goldman Sachs agreed to acquire LCN Capital Partners, a New York–based investment manager specializing in sale-leaseback, build-to-suit, and triple-net lease structures, for up to $410 million. LCN oversees approximately $3 billion in assets under supervision as of mid-2026, sourced from institutions, insurers, and high-net-worth individuals. The deal expands Goldman's private real estate platform and broadens its ability to serve insurance and institutional segments.
stories.impact: Modest relevance to multifamily. Consolidation of SLB and BTS capital into mega-platforms may reduce competition for deal flow and increase pricing on corporate/industrial sale-leasebacks, but doesn't directly reshape multifamily acquisition or development capital dynamics. However, if GS deploys more capital into net lease and SLB, competitive pressure on multifamily cap rates could ease as capital rotates.

stories.title: AI-Searched Public Records Alone Insufficient for Title Decision-Making: Study
stories.excerpt: Artificial intelligence-only searches of public records aren’t enough to provide reliable title decision-making at scale, according to a new study by DataTrace, a national provider of property and ownership data and title automation solutions. The company’s analysis, “AI Title Search Tested in the Real World: What Accuracy, Risk and Readiness Really Look Like,” compares AI-only with title plant-supported searches to evaluate completeness, accuracy and insurability. (A title plant is an index of all of the recorded events that affect a property, unique in that it’s posted, or indexed, as the official legal description of the property.) “The study is a projection of potential risk, and the opportunity to look at specific — what we would call, gaps — where the AI solution alone was used,” said Annette Cotton, senior vice president and chief data officer at DataTrace. “It predicts if that property had been insured upon, for instance, what could have been an outcome in terms of not being able to report on, address, or remediate that gap. “Our analysis demonstrates that AI performs best when it operates on a foundation of structured, validated title data, rather than fragmented county-level public records. The speed of AI creates value, but only when paired with the confidence, completeness and accuracy needed for insurable title decisioning. The future isn’t AI versus title professionals. It’s AI powered by trusted title data and guided by experienced title experts. That’s how the industry scales automation without sacrificing confidence or insurability.” DataTrace manages more than 2,000 title plants nationally. The new study is a follow-up to DataTrace’s first white paper on its position concerning title plant value, said Cotton. “This was intended to try to answer more details about that and what the impact would have been based on those early findings when we were doing the AI testing against traditional examination.” Among the current study’s
bullets: DataTrace study: AI-only title searches lack accuracy for insurance decisions.
AI performs best on structured data; title plants remain necessary.
Highlights gaps in AI-only approach that could create title risk.
stories.summary: A DataTrace study comparing AI-only title searches with title plant–supported searches found that artificial intelligence alone is insufficient for reliable title decision-making at scale. AI performs best when operating on structured, valid data; reliance on AI-only searches exposes properties to gaps that could result in uninsured title defects. The research suggests hybrid approaches—AI plus title plant indexing—are necessary.
stories.impact: Limited direct impact on multifamily development. However, land acquisitions and entitlement processes hinge on clean title. Developers relying on cost-cutting AI-only due diligence may face title defects, insurance denials, or refinancing complications late in project delivery. Due diligence discipline remains critical, particularly in markets with complex or older title histories (Northeast, Midwest).

stories.title: SFR Leasing Operating System Boom Secures $15M Series A Funding
stories.excerpt: Boom, a leasing operating system for single family rentals (SFR), announced Tuesday that it has secured $15 million in Series A funding. The company also announced the launch of BoomCRM, an agentic leasing and touring customer relationship management product built on top of the Boom’s existing underwriting engine. S3 Ventures led the round, with Mischief VC (fund of Plaid CEO Zach Perret) participating. Repeat participation came from venture capital firms Starting Line VC, Company Ventures, and Gilgamesh Ventures. Founded in 2020 and based in Austin, Texas, Boom bills itself as a financial services infrastructure company for rental operations. It works with property management systems dealing with on-time payments, fraud reduction and revenue growth across the renter lifecycle for SFR, scattered site and manufactured housing (MH) sectors. “We have been fairly conservative to date on the capital we’ve raised and the capital we’ve spent,” said Rob Whiting, CEO and co-founder at Boom. “We have a strong product market fit and have grown about 8x up until our Series A, and we’ve further grown 3x since the start of the year. This funding will help us accelerate several things, including the launch of this product and several more products after this, as well as growing the engineering team to support that, along with go-to-market efforts. As we primarily play in single-family rentals and manufactured housing, we want to continue to double down in those areas.” Boom’s existing products are BoomReport, automated rent reporting to incentivize on-time payments, grow revenue, and build resident credit, and BoomScreen, a tenant screening tool to mitigate fraud, increase leasing velocity, and move in best-qualified renters. Whiting said that most leasing CRMs today are either built multifamily-first or are general-purpose tools such as Salesforce and HubSpot, retrofitted for rentals. bullets: Boom (SFR leasing OS) raises $15M Series A; grown 8x pre-round, 3x post.
BoomCRM product launched: agentic AI for leasing and tenant CRM.
S3 Ventures led; tech infrastructure for SFR, scattered-site, MH sectors.
stories.summary: Boom, an Austin-based leasing operating system for single-family rentals, announced $15 million Series A funding led by S3 Ventures. The company has grown approximately 8x since founding and 3x since Series A close. Boom also launched BoomCRM, an AI-powered customer relationship management tool for leasing and touring. The platform serves SFR, scattered-site, and manufactured housing operations, focusing on underwriting, payment processing, and fraud reduction.
stories.impact: Indirect relevance to multifamily developers. SFR and scattered-site platforms compete for capital and operational efficiency. If Boom's AI-powered leasing and revenue management tools become standard in SFR, they may compress SFR operating margins, making single-family rental strategies less attractive relative to stabilized multifamily. However, for multifamily operators considering hybrid SFR portfolios, Boom's tech could reduce leasing and compliance overhead.

stories.title: Vantage Data Centers, Nebius Partner on AI Infrastructure at South Wales Campus
stories.excerpt: Denver-based Vantage Data Centers and Amsterdam-based artificial intelligence infrastructure company Nebius announced an agreement to deploy high-density, NVIDIA-powered AI infrastructure at Vantage’s CWL1 campus in Newport, Wales, one of Europe’s largest data center campuses. The deployment represents the first announced commercial capacity commitment in the South Wales AI Growth Zone and will support growing UK demand for domestic AI compute capacity. Under the agreement, Nebius will lease high-density capacity at CWL1 to support AI training, inference, agentic AI and enterprise AI workloads, serving enterprises, researchers, startups and public sector organizations seeking access to advanced AI infrastructure. “This is an important milestone for South Wales and for the UK’s AI infrastructure ambitions,” said David Howson, president, EMEA, Vantage Data Centers. “Nebius is scaling AI cloud infrastructure in the UK at a time when demand for domestic compute capacity continues to accelerate. Vantage’s Newport campus provides the scale, connectivity and operational excellence needed to support that growth, and we’re proud to help establish South Wales as a leading destination for AI investment.” South Wales was designated as a UK AI Growth Zone in recognition of its concentration of digital infrastructure, fiber connectivity to London, high-capacity electricity grid infrastructure and strong industrial base. The region is also home to the UK’s largest cluster of semiconductor businesses. The post Vantage Data Centers, Nebius Partner on AI Infrastructure at South Wales Campus appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Vantage Data Centers and Nebius deploy NVIDIA AI at CWL1, Newport, Wales.
First announced commercial capacity in UK AI Growth Zone.
Supports UK domestic AI compute demand; large-scale infrastructure play.
stories.summary: Denver-based Vantage Data Centers and Amsterdam-based Nebius announced a deployment of high-density, NVIDIA-powered AI infrastructure at Vantage's CWL1 campus in Newport, Wales—one of Europe's largest data center complexes. This is the first announced commercial capacity commitment in the newly designated UK AI Growth Zone. Nebius will lease capacity to support AI training, inference, and enterprise workloads for enterprises, researchers, startups, and public sector customers.
stories.impact: No direct impact on multifamily. However, large data center deployments can signal regional economic acceleration and talent migration. If South Wales becomes a UK AI hub, downstream demand for residential rental housing (for relocated tech workers and their families) could emerge—a leading indicator for multifamily developers tracking UK or European markets, but outside TCR's typical U.S. footprint.

stories.title: Corpay’s Cross-Border Business Leases Prebuilt at Rudin’s 560 Lexington
stories.excerpt: Rudin announced a new 11-year office lease with Corpay, Inc.’s. Cross-Border business at 560 Lexington Ave., its 22-story office tower in the Plaza District. Corpay Cross-Border Solutions, which specializes in foreign exchange, global payments and risk management, will relocate its headquarters to 560 Lexington this fall. The company will occupy a 17,778-square-foot prebuilt space spanning the entire 17th floor of the 380,000-square-foot building. “Corpay’s commitment to 560 Lexington demonstrates the continued allure of the Plaza District and further validates our investments in our portfolio’s amenity and prebuild programs,” said Kevin Daly, VP of office leasing at Rudin. “Given these ongoing efforts, only minor modifications to a prebuilt floor were needed to meet Corpay’s requirements. This allowed us to accommodate their accelerated timeline for move-in, which was a big factor in getting the deal done.” Jacob Rosenthal and Kevin Carroll of CBRE represented Corpay. Rudin was represented in-house by Daly and a CBRE team of Peter Turchin, Brett Shannon, Eric Deutsch and Lauren Levy. The post Corpay’s Cross-Border Business Leases Prebuilt at Rudin’s 560 Lexington appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Corpay Cross-Border Solutions leases 17,778 SF at Rudin's 560 Lexington.
11-year lease; entire 17th floor; headquarters relocation this fall.
Prebuilt space enabled accelerated move-in; Plaza District office demand sustained.
stories.summary: Rudin Management secured an 11-year office lease with Corpay, Inc.'s Cross-Border business for 17,778 square feet spanning the entire 17th floor of 560 Lexington Avenue in Manhattan's Plaza District. Corpay, which specializes in foreign exchange, global payments, and risk management, is relocating its headquarters to the space this fall. Rudin's prebuilt floor program allowed minor modifications and accelerated occupancy.
stories.impact: No direct impact on multifamily. However, sustained office leasing (even at trophy addresses) by corporate tenants signals selective demand for prestige Manhattan office space. This may reduce pressure on Class A office conversion-to-residential pipelines in Midtown/Plaza District and slow multifamily supply in that micromarket—a slight tailwind for existing and future multifamily assets in adjacent neighborhoods where office conversion risk is higher.

stories.title: Marcus & Millichap’s Azzi Group Closes Value-Add Sale of West Hollywood Multifamily
stories.excerpt: Marcus & Millichap closed the sale of 1203 N. Kings Road, a 30-unit multifamily property in West Hollywood. The property sold for $7.98 million, or $266,000 per unit. “The property presented the buyer with a rare opportunity to acquire a well-located West Hollywood asset at an attractive basis with significant value-add potential,” said Tony Azzi, executive managing director investments. “With opportunities to renovate vacant units and improve operations, the buyer is well positioned to enhance the property’s long-term cash flow. West Hollywood continues to benefit from strong rental demand driven by limited housing supply, walkability and access to major employment and lifestyle destinations throughout Los Angeles,” added Rabbie Banafsheha, senior director investments. Azzi and Banafsheha, of The Azzi Group in Marcus & Millichap’s Los Angeles office, marketed the property on behalf of the seller. Azzi, Banafsheha, Arteen Zahiri and Ian Habbestad, also of The Azzi Group, procured the buyer. The conversations behind tomorrow’s apartment deals happen at Connect Apartments on September 22 in LA. Connect with the capital sources, owners, developers, and brokers driving multifamily investment. Learn more and reserve your seat at www.connectapts2026.com. The post Marcus & Millichap’s Azzi Group Closes Value-Add Sale of West Hollywood Multifamily appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Marcus & Millichap: 30-unit West Hollywood sale at $266K/unit ($7.98M).
Value-add play; vacant unit renovation and operational upside.
West Hollywood: limited supply, strong rental demand, walkability anchor.
stories.summary: Marcus & Millichap's Azzi Group closed the sale of 1203 N. Kings Road, a 30-unit multifamily property in West Hollywood, for $7.98 million ($266,000 per unit). The buyer acquired the asset as a value-add opportunity with upside from unit renovations and operational improvements. The broker commentary notes West Hollywood's tight supply and strong rental demand driven by walkability and proximity to major LA employment and lifestyle centers.
stories.impact: West Hollywood submarket (Los Angeles) remains supply-constrained and rental-demand-strong, supporting continued value-add acquisition and renovation activity. Per-unit pricing of $266K suggests modest cap rates after value-add exit—consistent with constrained LA supply and institutional buyer competition. For TCR developing in LA, this validates continued focus on supply-limited, high-amenity submarkets where pricing power and lease growth offset construction cost inflation.

stories.title: Northmarq Arranges $75M Acquisition Loan for Grocery-Anchored Queens Center
stories.excerpt: Northmarq’s New York Debt + Equity team led by Robert Delitsky and Keith Braddish arranged a $75-million loan for the acquisition and redevelopment of Whitestone Shopping Center, a 119,584-square-foot grocery-anchored shopping center located at 153-17 Cross Island Pkwy. in Whitestone, Queens. Northmarq arranged financing on behalf of BTF Whitestone LLC after running a marketing process with the lending community. Northmarq and ownership selected Acadia Realty Trust. The principals of BTF Whitestone LLC are Aaron Malinsky and Kenneth Schuckman. “After being overlooked for decades, Whitestone Shopping Center is about to undergo a significant transformation that will benefit both its tenants and the surrounding community,” said Delitsky. “Kenneth Schuckman and Aaron Malinsky are the ideal developers to restore Whitestone Shopping Center into a vibrant neighborhood retail destination.” The center is anchored by Key Food Supermarket, with additional tenants including Webster Bank and JPMorgan Chase. The post Northmarq Arranges $75M Acquisition Loan for Grocery-Anchored Queens Center appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Northmarq arranges $75M acquisition loan for Whitestone Shopping Center, Queens.
119,584 SF grocery-anchored center; Key Food anchor; redevelopment by BTF.
Queens retail financing active; repositioning overlooked shopping center asset.
stories.summary: Northmarq's New York Debt + Equity team arranged a $75 million acquisition and redevelopment loan for Whitestone Shopping Center, a 119,584-square-foot grocery-anchored center in Queens anchored by Key Food Supermarket, with co-tenants including Webster Bank and JPMorgan Chase. BTF Whitestone LLC, led by Aaron Malinsky and Kenneth Schuckman, acquired the asset. Acadia Realty Trust is the lender. The transaction signals redevelopment activity in overlooked Queens retail corridors.
stories.impact: Modest relevance to multifamily. Queens retail redevelopment capital availability suggests lender confidence in outer-borough NYC fundamentals. If Whitestone's repositioning succeeds (e.g., adding residential mixed-use components, generating foot traffic), it could strengthen residential rental demand in surrounding Whitestone neighborhoods, supporting future multifamily ground-up or conversion plays in Queens. However, financing is anchored to retail, not residential.
